c.tagline: Where the Blue and White Nile meet in the desert.

taxi.fareNote: Meters exist but are often ignored; agree the fare with the driver before departing, especially as a foreigner.

emergency.note: Emergency response can be slow, especially outside central districts; hospitals (e.g. Royal Care International Hospital, Fedail Hospital) and your hotel front desk are often the fastest first point of contact.

avoid.reason: The entire city is effectively off-limits — active armed conflict since April 2023 makes all travel to Khartoum unsafe.
Ongoing fighting, checkpoints, looting and lawlessness make any movement in the city dangerous.

hood_desc: The government quarter at the confluence of the Blue and White Nile, holding the Presidential Palace and the landmark Corinthia tower. It was fought over and heavily damaged between 2023 and 2025, and only a small part of its hotel stock has been brought back into service.
A leafy, comparatively upscale district along Africa Road with international restaurants, offices and NGO compounds; good for longer-stay business visitors who want a quieter residential feel.

water.note: Tap water is not recommended for visitors; stick to bottled or treated water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (Sudanese pounds) directly to the driver or conductor; there is no unified electronic fare card. Amjad minibus and riksha fares are not metered, so agree the price before boarding.
transit.hours: Buses and minibuses generally run around 06:00-22:00; after dark, ride-hailing apps (Tirhal, Mishwar) or a pre-arranged taxi are the safer option.
transit.note: Public transport is informal with routes not signed in English; rickshaws/tuk-tuks are barred from central downtown streets and from crossing the Nile bridges.

train: Sudan Railways (limited passenger service to Atbara, Port Sudan and northern towns)
bus: Private long-distance coaches to Port Sudan, Kassala, El Obeid and other regional cities
ferry: Tuti Island ferry across the Blue Nile
Seasonal Nile ferries linking Khartoum, Omdurman and Bahri

airport.name: Khartoum International Airport
airport.drive: 10-15 min from downtown Khartoum (Al Mogran) in normal traffic, longer at security checkpoints

transit.m: Public bus into central Khartoum (about 45 min, infrequent)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% in restaurants and hotels is appreciated but not expected.

landmarks: Confluence of the Blue and White Niles
Watch two distinct-colored rivers merge into one at Al-Mogran, the dramatic natural spectacle that gives Khartoum its name and its most photographed view.
National Museum of Sudan
Home to relocated ancient Nubian temples and pharaonic treasures rescued from the Aswan Dam flooding, offering a sweeping journey through Sudan's millennia-old civilizations.
Republican Palace (Presidential Palace)
This grand colonial-era palace on the Blue Nile corniche marks the historic site of General Gordon's death and remains a stately symbol of Sudanese sovereignty.
Tomb of the Mahdi
This silver-domed mausoleum in Omdurman honors Muhammad Ahmad, the 19th-century Mahdist leader, standing as one of Sudan's most recognizable religious silhouettes.
Omdurman Souq
Wander a sprawling, chaotic market of spices, gold, textiles and camels that has been the beating commercial heart of Greater Khartoum for over a century.
Whirling Dervishes of Hamed al-Nil
Every Friday, Sufi dervishes in colorful robes spin into trance-like ecstasy at this Omdurman shrine, a mesmerizing spiritual spectacle beloved by photographers.
Khalifa House Museum
Once home to the Mahdi's successor, this mudbrick museum in Omdurman displays 19th-century weapons, manuscripts and artifacts from Sudan's revolutionary Mahdist era.
Tuti Island
A lush agricultural island sitting precisely at the Nile confluence, reachable by bridge or ferry, offering village life and panoramic river views just steps from downtown.
Corinthia Hotel Khartoum
This striking egg-shaped riverside tower has become Khartoum's unmistakable modern skyline icon, visible from nearly every vantage point along the Nile.
Great Mosque of Khartoum
The city's principal mosque anchors the historic downtown, its minarets and courtyards reflecting Khartoum's Islamic heritage amid the bustling capital streets.

train.note: Sudan Railways' passenger network was already largely defunct before the war, and amid the civil war that began in April 2023 there are no reliable scheduled passenger trains from Khartoum. The old Wadi Halfa-Khartoum train is reported discontinued. Travel to and within Sudan is currently inadvisable - check your government's advisories.

bus.note: No reliable, bookable scheduled international coaches operate from Khartoum; the conflict has severely disrupted road transport and closed or made routes dangerous. Before the war, buses ran north toward Wadi Halfa and the Egyptian border - confirm the security situation and any operating services locally before relying on them.

ferry.note: Khartoum is inland at the junction of the Blue and White Nile, with no sea access. The former Wadi Halfa-Aswan (Egypt) ferry across Lake Nasser is reported discontinued, and the Port Sudan-Jeddah (Saudi Arabia) sea ferry (historically Namma Shipping Lines) leaves from Port Sudan, roughly 800km east, with an uncertain wartime status - verify before planning.
